A tall portrait illustration made with a steel dip pen and diluted grey ink brushed wet onto brittle, tea-yellowed newsprint, so the paper's own grain and foxing show through the washes. We look down from a little above at a small public garden in 1919, early morning, swallowed by a dense, low, motionless fog. Visibility ends a few strides from the bench: iron railings and the trunks of plane trees are inked crisply at the front, then go faint, then become only pale smudges, then nothing, as if the wash has eaten them. One cast-iron park bench sits dead centre, the only thing drawn with full, hard, black line. On its left end sits a fat rich man in a long dark overcoat and a tall silk top hat, a heavy black mass laid down in dense crosshatching, a shade too large for the bench, which sags under him; the upper part of his hat bleeds softly upward into the grey fog with no edge. His face is half shadow, small pale eyes, a thin satisfied smile, and he lifts one fat gloved hand lazily from the wrist in a bored, dismissive brush-off. At the far right end, small and drawn in thin, broken, faltering line, a young soldier in a worn army greatcoat with one trouser leg pinned up and a wooden crutch beside him, his outline thinning into the mist as if he is already being erased. Flat, sourceless, shadowless dawn light; palette of ink black, three greys of wash and the yellow of old paper, nothing else. Wide empty fog fills the top third of the frame. No lettering, captions, signatures or text anywhere in the picture. Thanks.

One surviving frame of a lost 1919 horror reel, upright portrait framing. Night in a public garden, everything gone except a cast-iron bench and a single gas lantern hanging on a bracket straight above it, so its flame pours down like a spotlight from the ceiling of the dark. On the bench, directly under that flame, a bloated plutocrat in a stovepipe silk hat, black frock coat strained over his belly, a gold fob chain catching one spark. The overhead glare drops the hat brim's shadow across his eyes, leaving two bottomless black pits where they should be, while below them a powdered, chalk-pale face holds a courteous little smile that glows almost white; his lip rouge prints as ink, as red always did on that blue-only stock. Wearily, a gloved hand dangles and flaps once at the man beside him: a hollow-cheeked infantryman home from the front, army greatcoat too big, one leg ending at the knee with the trouser folded and pinned, a plain wooden crutch laid across his lap. The veteran sits past the edge of the lamplight and dissolves into the night, only his fingers on the crutch and the line of one cheekbone faintly showing. Static camera at seated eye level, square-on, a medium shot of the pair placed in the lower half of the frame, the upper third an unbroken black void above the lantern kept clear for a caption. The emulsion of a hand-cranked early nitrate print: blown-out whites slamming into pure black with almost nothing in between, coarse clotted grain, hairline scratches running top to bottom, flecks of dust, edges going soft, a round iris mask darkening all four corners. Monochrome, photochemical, no smooth digital finish, no lettering anywhere. Thanks.

A two-colour reduction linocut, rust-orange laid down first and heavy black printed over it from the same recut block, pressed onto coarse cream paper, the two inks sitting slightly out of register. There is no soft shading anywhere: every mark is a hacked, splintered gouge, raw and angry, as though carved in a hurry. We lie at gravel level on a park path in 1919, right beside the scuffed rubber foot of a wooden crutch looming huge and close in the lower left corner, and the whole view is tipped several degrees so the path climbs steeply away from us. High up and far off sits a park bench, drawn tiny and needle-sharp: a corpulent plutocrat wearing a towering stovepipe hat and a buttoned morning coat, flicking his fingers outward in a lazy brush-off, and beside him a gaunt veteran with a cropped head and a frayed khaki tunic, one leg ending at the knee, the empty trouser folded and pinned. Behind them a swollen dusk sun hangs low on the horizon, a burning orange disc with chiselled rays. From it the plutocrat's shadow spills down the path toward us, grotesquely oversized and stretched, the hat drawn out into a black chimney and the belly into a heaving blot, rearing over the seated veteran and running all the way down the gravel until it touches the crutch beside us. The veteran's shadow is only a frail cracked splinter. Leafless trees bend inward from both sides like bars. Above the bench, a wide strip of raw streaked orange sky stays completely empty. No writing, lettering, numbers or signs anywhere. Thanks.

Vertical night photo, lens wide open so only the closest subject holds focus. Close to camera, crisp down to the drizzle beads on her eyelashes, an exhausted nurse in wrinkled scrubs slouches against the armrest of a public bench, eyes shut, head lolling sideways, staff badge on a lanyard tangled around her collar, a paper face mask dangling from an ear, palms upturned and slack on her thighs. The bench is cast iron and timber slats, its green coat blistered and scabbed off in flakes over brown rust, puddles sitting in the gaps. Seated further down that very bench, a little behind her and smeared by the shallow focus into soft blobs, waits an enormous figure: dark bulky coat, a tall stovepipe hat, a pale round face with a broad white grin, and a raised palm flicking toward her in a dismissive wave. Out of focus he is mostly a heavy black silhouette; you have to squint to be sure he is real, and he seems to lean slightly closer than anyone should. One sodium-vapour streetlamp behind them drowns everything in flat amber monochrome, so colours die and skin turns waxy; its glow swells into a hazy halo in the fine mist, and beyond its reach the park sinks into murky darkness. The top third is empty black wet sky dissolving into haze. Palette of amber, rust brown and inky black, a hint of cold teal left in her scrubs; visible grain, bloom around the lamp, no text, signage or writing. Thanks.

Vertical black-ink drawing on off-white paper, a single face pressed so close to the viewer that it overflows every border: a plump, well-fed gentleman, ears and temples cropped away, nothing at all behind him but his own skin. Across the top edge lies the stiff brim of a tall silk hat, sealing him in like a coffin lid. His brow and both eye sockets are dug out with layer upon layer of short broken hatching strokes, each patch running a new direction, stacked until they read as near-solid black pits; lower down, across his cheeks, nose and heavy jowls, the strokes thin out into dense pinprick stipple, like pores under a magnifier. From the darkness of the left socket one eye stares out, rendered with fanatical precision, wet lid rims, single lashes, a hard white highlight on the cornea, and curled small inside that wet shine is his reflection of a lone exhausted nurse in rumpled scrubs sitting hunched on a slatted park bench, the only other living soul shown. His smile is courteous and much too broad, stretching nearly ear to ear, lips pulled thin over a tidy row of tiny matching teeth, cheeks puffed into hatched folds. Nib lines scratchy, occasionally splitting, the pressure relentless and obsessive. The drawing ends abruptly beneath his doubled chin and starched wing collar, leaving a wide strip of untouched paper along the bottom. Dead-centre, eye-level framing, claustrophobically near, shadowless even light where all darkness comes from the pen. Pure line and dot, no grey washes, no colour, no lettering. Thanks.
Old console game, he is too sharp

Still grabbed from a 1998 home-console horror game running at 320 by 240 pixels, a little before dawn: one public bench on a cracked tarmac path, watched by a camera fixed high up on a lamp post and pitched sharply downward, the angle of a cheap surveillance feed nobody checks. Everything is built from few polygons, with blunt angular limbs and corners that do not quite meet; tiny low-resolution textures are stretched across them and bend in the wrong directions, so the slats, the litter bin and the strip of grass look smeared and rippled; every shade is broken into a coarse checkerboard dither and every outline steps like a staircase. Two or three metres past the bench a dense grey-green haze stops the world dead, flat and featureless, filling the upper portion of the picture as blank space. On the left end of the bench a worn-out nurse in faded blue scrubs slumps forward with her elbows on her knees, lit by a single cold cone of light, her body as blocky and blurred as the bin beside her, her face only a few muddy pixels. On the right end, impossibly, sits an obese gentleman wearing a tall black silk hat and a heavy frock coat, rendered with photographic sharpness as though he belongs to a different, far more expensive machine: crisp wool weave, pin-sharp watch chain, damp pink skin, heavy chins, a thin patient smile, pale wet eyes lifted straight to the lens. His fingers rise lazily toward her, palm out, brushing her away. The sharpness is what makes him monstrous. Colours of mould, wet cement and old pond water, the nurse's light a dim fluorescent white. No words, numbers, logos, health bars or on-screen interface. Thanks.

Portrait-format oil painting done directly on a damp, ancient plaster wall: the surface is crazed with fine cracks, blistered and flaking, chalky bare ground breaking through the pigment in pale islands. Jammed against the right edge, a vast pot-bellied plutocrat squats forward on the last few slats of a park bench, swollen so large his shoulders seem to press out through the wall toward us. He wears a battered stovepipe hat and a long dark tailcoat swallowed by shadow; his doughy face is mud and ash, the eyes sunk into dark hollows with one wet point of light each, and a wide crooked grin of yellowed teeth splits it ear to ear. One heavy gloved hand floats up near his jaw, limp at the wrist, flicking a lazy, bored brush-off at nobody. Paint is slapped on fast with a broad brush and a palette knife, dragged, scraped back, left to drip down his coat. The single clean white in the whole picture is his starched shirt bib, glowing under the chins. Leftward the bench gives out after two slats and sinks into soot; everything else is an immense brushy darkness of umber and lamp-black, faint grey ghosts where earlier figures were painted out and lost, as if he alone outlived whatever else was on this wall. The top half is nearly empty smoky gloom, calm enough for a caption. Seen square-on and close, at standing height, as if in a dim room before the wall; a weak raking light from one side picks out the ridges of paint. Colours restricted to yellow ochre, raw umber, ash grey and black, plus that one white. No text, no lettering, no signature. Thanks.
Only he stays still (glass plate) ⚠ looks like a real politician

Tall antique silver-gelatin photograph printed from a cracked glass plate, shot by a big wooden view camera locked off at seated eye height, square-on to a cast-iron park bench with wooden slats that sits across the bottom half of the frame, deep focus from front to back. One man occupies the middle of the bench, perfectly frontal, full figure from hat to boots: enormously fat, wealthy, in a tall gleaming stovepipe hat, a frock coat straining over a waistcoat, a gold watch chain looped across his belly, gloved hands, polished spats. His right hand is raised beside his shoulder, palm out, mid-dismissal. He alone is razor sharp, every stitch and whisker crisp, with a wide, calm, unmoving smile and pale eyes that hold the lens without blinking. The plate was left open on a bright overcast day for so long that everyone who came and went has dissolved into translucent drifts of grey: ranks of marching soldiers, a man on a crutch, nurses in scrubs, shoppers, a pram, whirling leaves, layer upon layer of half-erased bodies streaming past and even sitting beside him, faint as fog on a window, none casting a shadow. Only the fat man casts one, a solid black blot under the seat. Tonal range runs from soot black to cold paper white with no colour. The plate itself is decaying: a bluish metallic silvering creeping in from the borders, thin scratches, dust specks, one corner broken off to clear glass, a spidery crack across a lower edge. The top third is an almost blank, blown-out pale sky with a couple of bare twig tips, kept clear. Unsettling through stillness, never gore. No writing, signage or letters. Thanks.

Portrait-format oil painting in a meticulous, technically exact dystopian surrealist manner: a vast, deep view looking down from high and far away over the remains of a public park, now a desert of drifted rust-coloured powder under a dull brown noon. Bent iron fencing curls over like dead fern fronds and sinks into the dunes; a lone stripped tree, charred and forked, claws at the haze; a fallen cast-iron lamp standard has turned to grey cinder along half its length and is crumbling where it lies. Everything far off melts into airborne grit, layered in fading veils of atmospheric perspective. The sun is a pale bruise behind the murk and the light is flat, heavy and shadowless. Colour is strictly limited to four neighbouring earth tones, yellow ochre, burnt sienna, raw umber and iron-oxide red, with a crusted, granular paint surface and dirty, unevenly overlapping hatch marks that read as grime built up over years. Precisely in the middle of the canvas, very small, sits an unbroken wooden park bench, and on it a stout, heavy-jowled gentleman wearing a tall silk stovepipe hat, an immaculate frock coat, a clean white collar and pale kid gloves, his skin rosy and smooth, untouched by the dust, the single bright, cool note in the entire painting. Knees crossed, he flicks the fingers of his right hand outward in a bored brush-off towards the vacant seat and the dead land, wearing a thin, contented smile, though there is not a living soul for miles to receive it. Overhead, the choking dun haze rolls on unbroken and featureless across a wide band of the picture, a blank stretch of murky air kept bare so words can be laid over it afterwards. The image holds no lettering, words, signs or numerals of any kind. Thanks.

A tall vertical drawing, pure black ink on cream newsprint, looking steeply down from a high vantage onto a small city park on a frozen January morning in 1919. The whole top third is open winter sky, pale and blank, untouched by the pen. Below it the park unfolds in exact two-point perspective: a curving gravel path dusted with hoarfrost, a row of leafless elms whose every twig is drawn as a fine forking line, a spiked iron railing receding toward the corner, one fluted gas lamp standing beside the path. Shadows and the dark bark are built from patient layered hatching, three and four directions deep, the frosted grass left as stippled white. Small in the lower third, seen from above, sits a single slatted wooden bench. A stout, bulging gentleman in a silk top hat and fur-collared overcoat sits bolt upright and spreads across most of its length, one gloved hand lifted, palm flat outward, brushing someone away. Squeezed onto the bench's last foot of seat, a thin young ex-soldier in a worn army greatcoat bends toward him, one trouser leg folded and pinned below the knee, a wooden crutch lying across his lap. A little cloud of breath hangs before each mouth, outlined in a few curling strokes. Cold flat morning light, no colour at all, the drawing reading like a careful plate from a period weekly. The image is drawing only, with no lettering, captions, numbers, or initials anywhere.

Upright magazine plate from 1919 rendered entirely in broad black grease crayon rubbed over thin grey ink washes on toothy, ridged board, so the darks crumble into a granular salt-and-pepper grain and every edge is soft, thumb-smudged and velvety, the feel of a lithograph rather than a pen line. The viewpoint is low and very near: filling the bottom of the picture, crisp and enormous, a fat kid-gloved hand with a starched cuff and a gold stud flicks the air outward, fingers fanned in a lazy brush-off frozen at its height. Tucked just behind it and still sharp, a portly magnate seen in profile, heavy jowls folding over a stiff collar, a clipped moustache, drowsy hooded eyes looking nowhere, a stovepipe hat polished to a shine, his elbow propped on the curled cast-iron arm of a park seat. Deeper in the picture, blurred and rubbed soft as though the crayon was wiped with a finger, a hollow-cheeked young private in a creased khaki tunic grips a wooden crutch, one leg ending at the knee with the trouser folded and pinned, his gaze locked on that waving hand. Late dusk: a lone gas lamp beyond the right edge rakes long slanted crayon shadows across the scene and catches a thin pale edge of bare paper on the hat brim and the knuckles. The top third of the image is an almost empty field of deep soot-grey evening tone with a few faint scratched twigs, quiet room for words to be laid over later. Colours limited to black, graphite grey and warm cream paper; the board stays free of any written word, numeral or mark of authorship. Thanks.

Upright newspaper cartoon from about 1919, inked quickly with a steel nib on smooth board and run off on cheap pulp stock that has browned to the colour of weak tea, with slight grain and a ghost of the reverse page bleeding through. The viewpoint is a few steps behind a slatted park bench at standing height, so both sitters face away from us. Right half of the seat: a colossal plutocrat shown only from the back, a black frock coat strained across shoulders broad as a sideboard, fat creasing over a stiff white collar, a gleaming stovepipe hat pushed back on his skull; his face is turned a fraction further away from his neighbour while one plump gloved hand swings out to the side at arm's length in an idle, can't-be-bothered brush-off. Left half: a slight young infantryman in a rumpled khaki tunic and peaked cap, back curved, chin dropped to his chest; a wooden crutch rests slanted against the slats by his hip, and under the seat a single hobnailed boot stands on the gravel where two should be, the empty trouser leg folded and pinned. Lines are swift, sure and mostly unbroken outline, with just a handful of hatch strokes in the coat creases and the bench boards. The sun sits straight overhead at midday, so each body drops a tight, solid black puddle directly beneath it and the rest of the scene stays almost unshaded. Behind the bench a bright gravel promenade runs off with promenaders in flat straw boaters, ladies under parasols and clipped plane trees, all touched in with faint, thin, scattered strokes so the two backs dominate. The bottom fifth is open, bare pale gravel, kept empty so words can be set there afterwards. Only black ink on warm browned cream. Nothing written, no balloons, no captions, no labels, no monogram drawn anywhere. Thanks.

Tall portrait poster image, styled after a turn-of-the-century German comic weekly printed by colour lithography: confident black brush contours of even weight, each shape filled with one flat, unmodulated ink, and only four inks used in total: black, sodium-lamp orange, clinical teal and an off-white like old newsprint. No tonal blends, no soft shading, no texture fills. The top band of the frame, roughly a fifth of its height, is pure flat black night with nothing in it, kept clear for a caption added later. Underneath, a straight-on eye-level view of a wooden park bench with curly iron arms on a paved forecourt outside a modern hospital at night: the automatic entrance doors read as a glowing off-white block, a flat canopy overhangs them, and the façade is a grid of teal cladding. Overhead on the right, a lamp on a tall post throws a sharp wedge of orange light over the bench, and the shadow beneath the seat is a single crisp black shape. Sprawled across two thirds of the seat, a portly tycoon dressed as in 1910, a tall black stovepipe hat, a long dark frock coat, a pale waistcoat strung with a gold watch chain, knees wide, belly pushed out, a self-satisfied round face; his near arm is stretched out sideways, hand open and palm towards the woman beside him in a dismissive wave. Squeezed onto the far end, a present-day nurse in teal scrubs and grubby white trainers, an ID lanyard round her neck, strands of hair slipping from a claw clip at the end of a night shift, cups a small paper vending-machine coffee in both hands and gazes straight ahead, worn out, paying his hand no attention. Exaggerated cartoon proportions for the two people, crisp simple geometry for the building, a fresh composition of our own. The picture carries no writing at all: no words, numbers, signs or signatures. Thanks.

Vertical drawing, eye-level medium two-shot of one weathered slatted bench at a present-day bus stop on a drizzly grey afternoon, two different hands of ink meeting in a single picture. He occupies the right side: a portly elderly plutocrat in a towering stovepipe hat, swallow-tailed coat buttoned tight over a round belly, gold fob chain, white spats, fat cigar pinched in jewelled fingers. He alone is drawn the old way, built from heavy hatched and cross-hatched strokes in warm brown-black on a slightly foxed, cream-coloured scrap of paper with a ragged scissor edge, so he reads as a figure cut from a hundred-year-old broadsheet and glued onto the page. Nose raised, eyelids lowered, staring off past the frame, he flaps the back of one gloved hand at her in a bored shooing gesture without sparing her a glance. On the left a worn-out nurse in her thirties, teal-blue scrubs beneath an unzipped NHS-style waterproof, ID badge on a lanyard, mobile screen lit in her palm, leans toward him mid-sentence with heavy eyes. She and the whole modern world around her — the glass shelter, kerbstones, puddles reflecting streetlight, a smeared red double-decker sliding past — are drawn in fine, steady, uniform contemporary pen line with gentle cool-grey watercolour washes and no hatching. Thin slanting rain lines fall over everything and bead on the slats. The top quarter of the frame is a plain, pale, washed-out grey sky left completely empty so words can be laid over it later. Palette: warm sepia-black for the gentleman only; cool greys, white paper and a single muted teal for her. Nothing written or printed anywhere in the picture. Thanks.

Vertical editorial cartoon drawn with a dip pen and India ink on cream bristol board, in the spirit of a weekly humour magazine from about 1915 but our own scene: confident tapering contour lines, cross-hatching for the darks, a pencil sketch faintly visible under the ink, and a thin cold wash of blue-grey and gunmetal brushed over it. We look past a nurse who sits on a park bench with her back to us: along the lowest part of the picture, her shoulder in plain hospital scrubs and the knot of her tied-back hair are sketched in a few loose, broken, unfinished strokes, like a near object out of focus. Sharp and large in the centre is the portly rich man beside her, turned toward her and toward us: a gleaming silk top hat, wing collar biting into a heavy jowl, a buttoned waistcoat stretched over his belly. He is mid-brush-off, eyelids drooping half closed with lazy contempt, a thick cigar parked at the side of his mouth, one gloved hand lifted with the palm turned up toward her, done with the conversation. It is just after sunrise and she has worked all night: a pale, low sun sits behind him so a thin line of untouched white paper traces the crown and brim of his hat and the curve of his shoulders, while his face falls into fine hatched shadow. Far behind the bench a modern skyline of glass office towers is suggested in faint hairlines, small and unimportant. The top quarter of the sheet is open, unwashed morning sky for a caption to sit on later. No lettering, speech balloons, signature or numbers drawn anywhere. Thanks.

Portrait-format page of warm ivory banknote stock, its upper third and lower third left completely bare, and between them a smooth unadorned ellipse containing a made-up gentleman engraved in the manner of an antique intaglio bill, one ink only, a dark bottle green so deep it reads almost black. He faces us dead centre, cropped just below the chest: a tall glossy silk topper, a broad well-fed face with a double chin spilling onto a starched high collar, a neat waxed moustache, narrow self-satisfied eyes meeting ours and a faint smug curl at the lips. One stubby gloveless hand is raised to his middle, thumb and finger pinching a heavy watch chain draped across a silk waistcoat, a dark tailcoat over it. The whole likeness is made of steady burin grooves: contour lines that swell and taper as they follow the roundness of cheek and forehead, a second set crossing them in the shadow beneath the brim and under the jaw, stippled dots and short dashes softening into bare paper on the highlights of nose and brow, long close-ruled strokes giving the hat its shine, near-solid crosshatch for the coat. Behind him, inside the ellipse, a quiet tint of fine horizontal rules that thins away toward the rim. No guilloche, no scrollwork, no lettering, no numerals, no seal, no serial, nothing written. Lighting is frontal and nearly shadowless, every feature crisp and legible like a character model sheet. A faint wipe of plate tone around the ellipse and the shallow pressed dent of the printing plate in the paper. Thanks.

A tall vertical sheet of old printed cartoon paper torn horizontally across its middle, the two pieces nudged back together so a ragged, fibrous rip zigzags from edge to edge, and through that rip shows a finger-wide strip of pale cream card, empty, reserved for a caption. Top piece, the year 1919: a wooden-slatted park bench with scrolled iron ends, inked in faded brown with a fine steel nib on grainy biscuit-toned stock; behind it a gravel walk, a low spiked railing, a gas lamp on a ribbed column, a bare elm, and far off a tiny lad pedalling a delivery bicycle. Nobody else on the bench; at its right-hand end slumps a portly tycoon, smooth-shaven, heavy jowls, a little pointed moustache, a polished silk top hat tipped forward over his right brow, a double-breasted frock coat tight across the belly, gold fob chain looped over the waistcoat, pale spats, a gloved hand capping a silver-headed walking stick stood between his knees, the other thumb tucked into a waistcoat pocket, eyes drooping with lazy self-satisfaction. Bottom piece, now: that exact bench from that exact viewpoint, inked by the same hand in sharp jet black on whiter stock, but its surroundings updated: a battered council bin, a thin modern street light with a flat LED head, square paving blocks, and a commuter in a hooded parka hurrying by, his face lit cold by the phone he stares at. On the right-hand end the tycoon sits again, an exact twin of the man above: jowls, moustache, hat tipped at precisely the same tilt, tight coat, fob chain, spats, stick, tucked thumb, drooping smug eyes, not one line older. Straight-on eye-level framing at sitting height, the bench drawn the same width in both pieces so its iron ends line up across the tear. One warm low sun from the left lights both centuries the same way, throwing long hatched shadows to the right; shading made of crosshatch and stipple, springy assured outlines, generous bare paper, the hand of a 1910s satirical magazine draughtsman. Every surface in the picture, sign, bin, phone screen and corner, stays bare of any marks: pure drawing. Thanks.

Hand-inked brush drawing with watery washes of warm sepia and slate grey on coarse cream paper, the look of a printed weekly paper's political sketch from just after the First World War, deliberately loose and personal rather than polished. Camera sits almost on the ground, low at the near end of a long gravel walk in a city park, staring along it to one plain wooden bench placed exactly in the middle of the picture, the walk's two edges narrowing toward it like rails. Alone on that bench, square in the centre, sprawls a plump, well-fed financier: a black stovepipe topper, a long dark morning coat buttoned over a round belly, a gold fob chain, white spats, one elbow hooked over the backrest and one ankle resting on a knee, smiling faintly with heavy-lidded eyes, untroubled, in no hurry, plainly expecting company. The planks to his left and to his right are empty. A sinking sun behind the lens throws his silhouette and the bench's into a single long black brushstroke that runs down the gravel toward us and almost reaches the bottom border. A handful of pigeons bob and peck around his gleaming patent-leather shoes, each bird a few quick flicks of the brush. The gravel nearest the lens melts into soft, puddled, out-of-focus wash; he and the bench are crisp, drawn in sure pen strokes with fine hatching shading the coat. Everything above the far treeline, the whole upper half of the tall frame, is a smooth sky wash grading from amber-sepia at the horizon to faint pearl grey at the top, utterly bare, no cloud, bird or branch, an open field reserved for overlay text that will be set in afterwards. Faint pale railings and leafless trunks sit low along the distant horizon. Mood: calm, golden, quietly menacing, an evening that ends with him still sitting there. Negative prompt: any writing, type, initials or markings drawn into the image. Thanks.
